Malignant tumors typically exhibit greater structural irregularity and are more likely to have high concavity values compared to benign tumors, which tend to have smooth, well-defined borders. Compared to 'mean concavity' and 'mean concave points', which represent average values, 'worst concavity' reflects the most severe pathological characteristics and is strongly correlated with malignant transformation in datasets like the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset.

While 'mean concavity' provides a general measure of concavity, it is less sensitive than 'worst concavity' because it averages across all tumor cells, smoothing out extreme cases. This can reduce its diagnostic power in early or subtle malignancies where 'worst' features are more critical.
